questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Model performance and purpose
questions.question: A food processor's model that flags contaminated batches reports 97% accuracy, but only 3% of batches in its test data were contaminated. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: The test data is too small because so few batches were contaminated
options.B: The accuracy figure was produced by the processor's own data team
options.C: The model needs monthly retraining to keep its accuracy current
options.D: The same 97% would result from flagging no batch at all

questions.key_concept: With rare events, high accuracy can hide a model that misses the cases that matter; fitness depends on purpose-relevant error rates.
questions.pre_read: Read every figure in the stem before judging what the reported score can show.
questions.correct_explanation: With only 3% of batches contaminated, a model that flagged no batch at all would still score 97%. The headline figure therefore cannot show whether the model finds contaminated batches, the one outcome the processor needs. Who produced the figure, option B, is the runner-up: independence matters, but an independently reproduced 97% would be just as misleading for this purpose.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because rare events feel like thin data. But the issue is imbalance, not size; even a large test set with 3% contaminated batches lets accuracy mislead.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because self-reported results are weaker evidence. But the deeper problem is the metric itself; reproducing 97% independently would not show the model finds contaminated batches.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models can drift. But nothing in the stem shows change over time, and retraining on a fixed schedule does not fix a misleading metric.

tips: Eliminate: A treats imbalance as a sample-size problem, and C prescribes retraining when the stem shows no drift, just a misleading metric.
Final two: D beats B because a misleading metric stays misleading whoever reproduces it; fitness is judged on the errors that matter, here missed contaminated batches.
Exam cue: when the event a model hunts for is rare, distrust overall accuracy and ask how many real cases it catches.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.2 (Potential costs of AI errors examined against risk tolerance)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Agentic AI considerations
questions.question: A travel company wants its customer-service assistant to rebook flights and issue refunds by itself, rather than just answer questions. Which consideration should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Whether the underlying language model scores well on public benchmarks
options.B: Whether customers are told that they are dealing with an AI assistant
options.C: Whether human approval is required above set payment and change limits
options.D: Whether a sample of the assistant's answers is checked for accuracy monthly

questions.key_concept: Agentic AI acts through tools and systems, so its key requirement is bounded authority with human approval above set limits.
questions.pre_read: Notice what new power the system gains in the stem, and ask what could go wrong once it can act rather than advise.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving from answering to acting makes this agentic AI: it now spends money and changes bookings through other systems. The most important control is a defined boundary on what it may do alone and when a person must approve. Disclosure to customers, option B, is the runner-up: transparency matters, but it does not stop a wrong refund or booking.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because strong benchmarks suggest a capable model. But public benchmarks say nothing about safe actions inside this company's booking and payment systems.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because people should know when AI serves them. But disclosure already mattered when it only answered questions; it does not limit refunds or bookings.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because output review is a common AI control. But checking answers misses the new risk: actions taken on bookings and payments.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on public benchmarks, which do not show safe behavior in this setting, and D reviews answers when the new risk lies in actions.
Final two: C beats B because once AI can act on money and records, limits and human approval prevent harm; disclosure informs customers but prevents nothing.
Exam cue: when an AI system gains the power to act, look first for limits on its actions and a person who approves or can stop them.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. One approval route for all AI uses
questions.question: A logistics firm's board-approved AI policy sends every AI use through one light approval step, from a meeting-notes summarizer to a model that screens job applicants. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the policy owner tier approval steps by each AI use's impact
options.B: Have the AI governance committee approve every AI use
options.C: Have HR suspend applicant screening until the policy is revised
options.D: Have IT review each AI tool's security before approval

questions.key_concept: An AI policy scales approval and oversight to each use's risk tier, set by impact on people and the business.
questions.pre_read: Read the policy rule and the uses it covers before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: An AI policy should scale its controls to each use's impact: a tool summarizing internal notes and a model screening job applicants carry very different risk to people. Risk tiers let low-impact uses move quickly and send high-impact ones to deeper review. Committee approval of every use, option B, is the runner-up: it adds rigor, but treating all uses alike swamps the committee and still ignores impact.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because committee review adds rigor. But approving every use alike wastes effort on trivial tools and still ignores which uses can harm people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because screening people is high risk. But suspending one use leaves the flat policy in place for every other high-impact use, so the cause stays unfixed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because security review is familiar. But security is one dimension; the gap is that approval ignores harm to people from AI decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C suspends one use and leaves the flat policy unfixed, and D reduces AI approval to a security check.
Final two: A beats B because approval effort should follow each use's impact; sending everything to the committee is uniform, not risk-based.
Exam cue: when an AI policy treats every use alike, recommend risk tiers that scale approval and review to impact on people and the business.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.3 (Level of risk management activity set by risk tolerance); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.4 (Risk management process established through transparent policies and controls)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Policy duties for staff
questions.question: A telecom company's AI policy requires staff to check generative AI drafts for invented facts, but training covers only tool use, and most drafts go out unedited. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the vendor add a policy reminder banner to every draft
options.B: Have team leaders sample sent replies monthly for unchecked drafts
options.C: Have IT limit the tool to staff who finished the tool training
options.D: Have the policy owner add the checking duty to the training

questions.key_concept: Awareness and training must teach the specific duties the AI policy imposes; detective sampling is a backstop, not the fix.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the policy requires with what people are taught, and ask where the gap starts.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness must match the policy. Staff must catch invented facts but were never taught how, and drafts going out unedited suggest they trust fluent AI output. Adding the checking duty to training fixes the cause. Sampling sent replies, option B, is the runner-up: it is a useful detective control, but it finds unchecked drafts only after customers have received them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a reminder is cheap and visible. But a banner does not teach staff how to spot invented facts, and people soon click past it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because monitoring shows whether the policy works. But it detects failures after customers are affected and leaves the training gap that causes them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it restricts the tool to trained users. But tool training teaches tool skill, not the checking duty the policy requires.

tips: Eliminate: A adds a reminder banner, which does not teach how to spot invented facts, and C limits use to tool-trained staff, though tool training is the gap.
Final two: D beats B because aligning training with the policy prevents unchecked drafts at the source; sampling sent replies detects them afterward.
Exam cue: when staff accept AI output unedited and training skips the policy's duty, recommend that the policy owner align training with that duty.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.2 (AI risk management training for personnel and partners); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AT-2 (Literacy Training and Awareness)

Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA pilot, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test, standards audit, concept review).

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. New AI laws
questions.question: An airline learns that a new AI law in one of its markets treats its crew-rostering model as high risk. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Switch off the model in that market until the law is clarified
options.B: Buy a compliance tool that scans each model against AI regulations
options.C: Have legal counsel and the model owner map each duty to controls
options.D: Apply the new law's requirements to every AI system worldwide

questions.key_concept: New AI obligations are mapped to controls, owners and evidence first; strategy and tooling choices follow the mapping.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the organization must know about the new duties before any response can be judged adequate.
questions.correct_explanation: The first step is to know exactly which duties apply to this model and whether controls already meet them. Mapping each obligation to a control, an owner and evidence shows the gaps to close. Applying the law everywhere, option D, is the runner-up: a global baseline can be a sound strategy, but it is a later management choice that still needs the mapping first.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it avoids exposure. But a high-risk label usually adds duties rather than banning use, and switching off a working model is management's decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because tools track regulations. But a tool cannot decide applicability, assign owners or produce evidence; governance comes before tooling.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because one standard is simpler. But extending duties worldwide is a strategy choice for management, and it still requires knowing the duties first.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a high-risk label as a ban, when such laws mostly add duties, and B buys tooling before anyone has decided which duties apply.
Final two: C beats D because a worldwide rollout still depends on knowing each duty and its control gap; mapping comes first and informs management's strategy.
Exam cue: when a new AI law applies, map each obligation to a control, owner and evidence before choosing tools or strategies.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements understood and managed)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Generative AI answers
questions.question: A labor ministry's staff believe its generative AI chatbot looks up current wage rules when workers ask questions, but it is connected to no document source. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Workers may not be told that they are chatting with an AI
options.B: The wage-rules database may be unavailable during busy periods
options.C: Workers may get confident answers matching no wage rule in force
options.D: The chatbot may word the same answer differently each time

questions.key_concept: Generative AI predicts plausible text rather than looking facts up, so answers not grounded in checked sources can be confidently wrong.
questions.pre_read: Ask how this kind of AI produces an answer, and compare that with what the staff believe it does.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model with no document source does not look rules up; it predicts plausible text from patterns in its training data, so answers can be outdated or invented. Workers may act on confident but wrong wage answers. Disclosure, option A, is the runner-up: workers should know they are using AI, but knowing does not make a wrong wage rule right.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because workers should know they are using AI. But disclosure does not stop the chatbot stating wage rules that do not exist.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because lookups depend on a database. But this chatbot is connected to no source; it generates answers, so database availability is not the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because varied wording looks unreliable. But different phrasing of a correct rule harms no one; the risk is content that is wrong.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes a database lookup the chatbot never makes, and D worries about wording, which harms no one when the content is right.
Final two: C beats A because generative AI can state invented or outdated rules with confidence; disclosure informs workers but does not make answers correct.
Exam cue: a generative model predicts plausible text; unless it is grounded in checked sources, expect confident errors, not lookups.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Systems combining two kinds of AI
questions.question: A Jamaican apprenticeship program's predictive model scores applicants, and a generative model then writes each rejection letter's reasons from the application. Which concern should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: The stated reasons may not reflect what actually drove each score
options.B: Drafted reasons holding personal data may be kept longer than needed
options.C: The scoring model may be less accurate for some groups of applicants
options.D: The two models may come from vendors with different contract terms

questions.key_concept: A generative model writes plausible text, so reasons it drafts may not match what a separate predictive model actually used to score.
questions.pre_read: Notice how many AI systems the stem describes, and what each one does with the applicant's file.
questions.correct_explanation: The score comes from the predictive model, but the reasons come from a generative model reading the application, which produces plausible text rather than tracing the score's drivers. Applicants may get reasons that are fluent but false, which undermines any appeal. Unequal accuracy across groups, option C, is the runner-up: it deserves testing, but nothing here points to it, while the letter design builds in the mismatch.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because drafted reasons hold personal data. But over-retention is a records-management risk, smaller than telling applicants reasons that did not drive their rejection.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because scoring models can treat groups unequally. But nothing here suggests it, while the letter design itself separates the stated reasons from the score.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because two suppliers mean two contracts. But contract terms are a third-party question; they do not affect whether letters state the true reasons.

tips: Eliminate: D is a supplier-terms question, and B is a records-retention point; neither affects whether applicants are told the true reasons.
Final two: A beats C because the design lets a generative model write plausible reasons the score never used; group accuracy deserves testing but has no support here.
Exam cue: when one AI system decides and another explains, check that the explanation is built from the decision's real drivers.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.5 (Explainable and Interpretable); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Ranking reader comments
questions.question: A news publisher's model ranks comments so the most useful appear first; trained on reply counts, it predicts them with 91% accuracy on held-out comments. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: Readers may not know that a model ranks the comments they see
options.B: The 91% accuracy may fall as news topics shift over time
options.C: The training set may hold too few months of past comments
options.D: The training label may not match the ranking's business goal

questions.key_concept: A model learns the label it is trained on; a proxy label can make it accurate at the wrong thing.
questions.pre_read: Read the whole stem before deciding what the 91% figure shows.
questions.correct_explanation: A model optimizes the label people give it. Reply counts are only a proxy for usefulness, and heated comments often draw the most replies, so 91% accuracy shows the model is good at the wrong thing. Drift, option B, is the runner-up: topics do shift and accuracy needs monitoring, but monitoring would only keep the model good at predicting replies, not usefulness.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because transparency matters. But telling readers a model ranks comments does not fix a model trained toward the wrong goal.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models drift as topics change. But monitoring drift would only keep the model good at predicting replies, not at finding useful comments.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models learn from data. But more months of reply counts would only teach the model the wrong goal more firmly.

tips: Eliminate: A is a disclosure point that leaves the wrong objective in place, and C worries about data volume, though more reply data only teaches the wrong goal more firmly.
Final two: D beats B because drift monitoring keeps a model good at its learned target; the reply-count label itself is the root problem.
Exam cue: a high accuracy score shows a model predicts its label well; check that label against the business goal before trusting the score.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.4 (Business value or context of use defined or re-evaluated); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Long reliance on an AI model
questions.question: A weather service's AI nowcasting model has drafted every storm warning for six years, and the continuity plan assumes forecasters will warn manually if it fails. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: The model may drift as storm patterns shift from its training data
options.B: Forecasters may resist plans to automate more of their warnings
options.C: The continuity plan may lack sign-off from the board
options.D: Forecasters may no longer be able to warn without the model

questions.key_concept: Long reliance on AI erodes the manual skills that fallback plans assume, so workforce plans must keep those skills current.
questions.pre_read: Read the model's history and the continuity plan together before weighing each risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The continuity plan relies on forecasters warning without the model, but for six years the model has drafted every warning, so manual skills may have faded or never formed in newer staff. If the model fails during a storm, the fallback may not work. Drift, option A, is the runner-up: it is a real AI risk, but nothing here shows it, and a failing model is exactly when the fallback must work.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models degrade as conditions change. But nothing here shows drift, and if the model did fail, the manual fallback is what must work.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because automation unsettles staff. But resistance is a change-management concern, smaller than a fallback that may fail during a storm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because plans need approval. But continuity plans are approved by management; board sign-off would not restore forecasters' manual skills.

tips: Eliminate: B is a change-management worry about staff acceptance, and C asks for board sign-off of an operational plan, which management approves.
Final two: D beats A because the plan assumes manual skills that six years of AI drafting may have eroded; drift has no support here.
Exam cue: when AI has done a task for years, ask whether people can still do it by hand before trusting a manual fallback.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Data quality for training
questions.question: A bus operator will redesign routes with a demand model trained on its smartphone app's trip logs, which the data owner has checked as complete and accurate. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The app's trip records used for training may not be encrypted
options.B: Riders' habits may shift once the redesigned routes begin
options.C: Riders who never use the app are absent from the training data
options.D: The quality checks were run by the data owner, not independently

questions.key_concept: Data can be complete and accurate yet unrepresentative; quality rules for training data must ask who is missing from it.
questions.pre_read: Read what the data owner's checks covered before weighing each concern.
questions.correct_explanation: Records can be complete and accurate for app users while leaving out every rider who pays cash or has no smartphone, often older or lower-income people. Routes planned from that data may serve them worse. Quality rules must cover representativeness. Independent checks, option D, are the runner-up: independence strengthens evidence, but checking completeness and accuracy again would not reveal who is missing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because trip data needs protection. But encryption is a security control; it does not change who the training data leaves out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because habits change with new routes. But that is a later monitoring question; the data is skewed before any route changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners checking their own data is weaker evidence. But an independent check of completeness and accuracy would still miss riders the app never records.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security control that leaves the data's coverage unchanged, and B is a later monitoring question, while the skew exists now.
Final two: C beats D because rechecking completeness and accuracy, however independently, cannot show riders the app never captured; representativeness is a separate test.
Exam cue: complete and accurate is not the same as representative; ask who never appears in the data the model learned from.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Customer records in prompts
questions.question: A seafood exporter's support copilot sends each customer's full account record, bank details included, to a hosted language model with every query, though most concern shipment status. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt traffic between the copilot and the model provider
options.B: Have the business owner pseudonymize customer names in each prompt
options.C: Have the vendor mask bank details in the copilot's answers
options.D: Have the business owner limit prompts to fields each task needs

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design for AI starts with minimization: prompts should carry only the personal data the task needs.
questions.pre_read: Read the copilot's design in the stem before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Every query sends bank details the hosted model never needs to answer a shipment question, so they leave the exporter's control each time. Privacy by design starts with minimization: send only the fields each task needs. Pseudonymizing names, option B, is the runner-up: it lowers identifiability, but bank details and the rest of the record still reach the provider.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects customer data. But it guards the data on the way; the provider still receives every bank detail in full.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pseudonymizing is a privacy technique. But bank details and the rest of the record still reach the provider, though the query never needs them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because output filters are a common AI safeguard. But masking answers does nothing about the full records sent in every prompt.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts data in transit, but the provider still receives it, and C masks answers while full records still go out in every prompt.
Final two: D beats B because sending only the fields a task needs keeps bank details from the provider; pseudonymizing names still sends them.
Exam cue: privacy by design for AI starts with the prompt; expect data minimization before filters, encryption or vendor promises.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Chatbots gaining new functions
questions.question: A Uruguayan sports federation's member chatbot, inventoried as a low-risk question-answering tool, can now cancel athlete registrations and waive license fees through federation systems. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner log each cancellation and fee waiver the chatbot makes
options.B: Have the owner retrain the chatbot to refuse risky requests
options.C: Have the owner reclassify it as agentic and reassess its risk tier
options.D: Have IT security test the chatbot's links to federation systems

questions.key_concept: An AI system that calls tools to change records is agentic; its classification and risk tier, not its underlying model, decide the controls it needs.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the chatbot before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Once the chatbot can cancel registrations and waive fees, it is agentic: it acts in federation systems instead of only answering. Its tier was set for a question-answering tool, so the owner must reclassify it and reassess its risk, which then decides the limits, approvals and oversight it needs. Logging every action, option A, is the runner-up: it records what the chatbot did, but only after registrations are canceled or fees waived.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs make an agent's actions traceable. But logging detects after the fact; the reassessed tier decides which preventive limits and approvals the chatbot needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a better-trained model errs less. But training cannot guarantee refusals; the reassessed tier must first decide which limits outside the model the chatbot needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because new system connections raise security risk. But security testing shows whether the links can be attacked, not what the chatbot may decide to do through them.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on retraining, which cannot guarantee refusals, and D tests security, which says nothing about what the chatbot decides to change.
Final two: C beats A because logs record actions after they happen; the reassessed tier decides which limits and approvals must stop wrong ones first.
Exam cue: when an AI system's inventory entry no longer matches what it can do, reclassify it and reassess its risk; the new tier sets its limits and approvals.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Risk tiers and human approval
questions.question: An Ivorian cocoa trader's AI policy rates any use low risk if a person approves each output, including a model ranking warehouse staff for redundancy. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the low tier, since a person makes each final redundancy decision
options.B: Have the policy owner drop the rule that approval lowers the tier
options.C: Have managers record a reason for each ranking they approve
options.D: Have IT review the ranking model's access controls and hosting

questions.key_concept: Tier AI uses by inherent risk, before controls; a human approval step is a control to judge, not a reason to lower a tier.
questions.pre_read: Read the policy rule and the use it covers before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A person approving each output does not make a use low risk: a wrong ranking can still cost staff their jobs, and approvers may simply accept what the model shows. Tiers follow each use's inherent risk, before any approval step, so the policy owner should drop the rule that approval lowers a tier. Option C, recorded reasons, is the runner-up: it may help review this model, but the rule still under-rates every approved use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a person signs each decision. But approval does not reduce the harm of a wrong ranking, and approvers often accept what the model shows.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because written reasons discourage rubber-stamping. But it treats one model, while the policy rule keeps rating every use with an approval step as low risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff data needs protection. But access and hosting reviews are security checks; they do not correct a tier that ignores impact.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a person's approval lowers the impact of a wrong ranking, and D reviews security, which does not correct how the use was tiered.
Final two: B beats C because the tiering rule under-rates every use with an approval step; recorded reasons may help this model but leave the rule in place.
Exam cue: a human approval step does not make an AI use low risk; tier each use by inherent risk, then judge the approval as a control.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Basis for accepting AI risk
questions.question: An Egyptian licensing board's exam face-verification model wrongly rejects candidates aged over 60 three times as often as others; the risk owner accepted it, citing 97% overall accuracy. What is the IS auditor's BEST action?

options.A: Reperform the 97% accuracy figure on recent check-in records
options.B: Report that the acceptance did not weigh harm to older candidates
options.C: Overturn the acceptance and suspend checks for older candidates
options.D: Leave the acceptance alone, since accepting risk is management's call

questions.key_concept: Risk owners choose the response, but an acceptance resting on overall accuracy that ignores harm to one group is uninformed and reportable.
questions.pre_read: Separate who decides the risk response from what the IS auditor checks about that decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk acceptance is the owner's call, but the IS auditor assesses whether it was informed. The 97% overall figure hides that candidates aged over 60 are wrongly turned away three times as often, a harm the acceptance never weighed, so the IS auditor reports it for the owner to reconsider. Reperforming the 97%, option A, is the runner-up: it checks the figure, but a correct overall figure would still hide the harm to older candidates.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reperformance is strong audit evidence. But a confirmed overall figure would still average away the higher error rate for candidates aged over 60.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the harm is clear. But overturning a risk acceptance or suspending the model is the owner's decision; the IS auditor reports and recommends.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because risk acceptance belongs to management. But the IS auditor still assesses whether the acceptance was informed and reports when it was not.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor overturning a decision that belongs to the owner, and D treats management's right to accept risk as putting its basis beyond audit.
Final two: B beats A because a correct overall figure would still hide the harm to older candidates; the gap is what the acceptance weighed, not the figure's accuracy.
Exam cue: an AI risk acceptance resting on one overall score is uninformed if one group bears more errors; report it and let the owner decide again.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.4 (Negative residual risks documented); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.1 Identifying and Assessing AI Risk (the risk owner chooses the response; the auditor assesses whether the assessment weighed harm to the people and groups affected). questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Shared foundation models
questions.question: A Canadian workers' compensation board finds its claims-review, call-center and fraud-detection vendors, which its continuity plan treats as independent, all use a single hosted language model. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: The vendors' controls reports may not cover the shared model provider
options.B: One provider's outage or update could disrupt three services at once
options.C: Staff may need training on three different vendor interfaces
options.D: The three vendors may give different answers about the same claim

questions.key_concept: AI supply chains run below the direct vendor; several vendors built on one model concentrate failure and change risk in a single provider.
questions.pre_read: Look past the three vendor names and ask what they have in common.
questions.correct_explanation: Three vendors that the continuity plan treats as independent share one dependency. An outage, a withdrawn model version or a silent behavior change at the provider would hit claims review, the call center and fraud detection together, so a plan that assumes one vendor fails at a time would not hold. Controls-report coverage, option A, is the runner-up: it is a real assurance gap, but the concentration exists whatever the reports cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fourth parties often fall outside vendor reports. But better reports would not remove the single point of failure shared by all three services.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because three interfaces add effort. But training cost does not threaten the services the way a shared failure would.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because inconsistent answers confuse injured workers. But inconsistency is a quality issue; a shared provider failing would stop all three services at once.

tips: Eliminate: D is a consistency issue, not a threat to the services, and C is a training cost that does not threaten them either.
Final two: B beats A because a shared model is a single point of failure across three services; better assurance reports would not remove it.
Exam cue: map AI supply chains below the direct vendor; several vendors on one model concentrate risk that contracts with each vendor do not show.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.12 (Value Chain and Component Integration); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.2 (Contingency processes for failures in high-risk third-party data or AI)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Licensed training data
questions.question: A Dubai property portal's valuation model was trained on a licensed sales-transactions dataset, and the license ends next month. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important to confirm?

options.A: Whether valuations stay accurate once the dataset is deleted
options.B: Whether the license lets the portal keep its published valuations
options.C: Whether the license lets the portal keep using models trained on it
options.D: Whether the dataset was kept encrypted during the license term

questions.key_concept: A trained model keeps what it learned, so data licenses must permit continued use of models trained on the data, not only its storage.
questions.pre_read: Read what happens when the license ends before weighing each question.
questions.correct_explanation: A trained model carries what it learned from the data, so deleting the dataset does not end the portal's use of that data. Whether models trained on licensed data may stay in use after the license ends depends on the license terms; if they forbid it, the model must be retired or retrained. Keeping published valuations, option B, is the runner-up: it is a real license question, but the model keeps producing new valuations daily.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data loss can affect models. But a model that is already trained does not change when its source data is deleted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because published valuations were derived from the data. But they are past outputs; the larger exposure is the model, which keeps producing new valuations from what it learned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because licensed data needs protection. But encryption during the term says nothing about whether use may continue after it ends.

tips: Eliminate: D concerns security during the license, not the right to keep using the data, and A assumes deleting the dataset changes a model already trained.
Final two: C beats B because the model keeps using what it learned to value new listings daily; published valuations are past outputs, a smaller exposure.
Exam cue: rights to use data for training must cover the trained model's life, not just how long the dataset is stored.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 4.1 (Legal and technology risks of components including third-party data mapped); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 6.1 (Policies address third-party AI risks including intellectual property)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (rights to use come from contracts and licenses; a trained model keeps what it learned after the data is gone). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Synthetic data from real records
questions.question: A Greek cancer registry plans to share synthetic patient records, produced by a generative model trained on its real records, with outside researchers as non-personal data. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have researchers sign agreements to keep the synthetic records secure
options.B: Test the synthetic records for close matches to real patients
options.C: Encrypt the synthetic records before sending them to researchers
options.D: Strip names and ID numbers from the real records before generating

questions.key_concept: Synthetic data from a generative model trained on personal records can reproduce real people, so it is tested before being treated as non-personal.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the generative model learned from, and whether its output could still describe a real patient.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model trained on real records can memorize and reproduce them, especially rare cases, so synthetic output is not automatically non-personal. Testing the synthetic records for near copies of real patients shows whether sharing them could identify anyone. Stripping names first, option D, is the runner-up: it removes direct identifiers, but a rare diagnosis with an age and a town can still identify a patient.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agreements bind researchers. But a contract does not settle whether the records identify patients; that needs testing first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because health data needs protection in transit. But encryption protects records on the way, not whether they describe real people.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing direct identifiers is standard de-identification. But the records are already generated, and rare combinations of diagnosis, age and place remain for the model to reproduce.

tips: Eliminate: C protects records in transit, not whether they describe real people, and A binds researchers without settling whether the data is personal.
Final two: B beats D because removing names leaves rare combinations a model can reproduce; only testing the output shows whether real patients appear.
Exam cue: synthetic data from a model trained on personal data stays a privacy question until tests show it does not reproduce real people.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 2.4 (Privacy Attacks and Mitigations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.2 Personal Data in Training, Prompts and Outputs (de-identified or derived data can still identify people; output from a model trained on personal data needs testing before sharing). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Reusing fine-tuned models
questions.question: A Lebanese bank's marketing team wants to build its campaign-writing model on a retired chatbot that was fine-tuned on customer service chats. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Encrypt the retired model's files before marketing copies them
options.B: Confirm the chat training set was securely deleted from every system
options.C: Test the retired model's writing on sample marketing campaigns
options.D: Have the data owner decide whether the chats may serve marketing

questions.key_concept: A model can memorize its training data, so reusing a model trained on personal data for a new purpose needs a data owner's decision.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the retired chatbot before weighing each step.
questions.correct_explanation: A model fine-tuned on customer chats can memorize and reproduce them, so building on it carries the chats into a new purpose, marketing. Whether that reuse is allowed is the data owner's decision, with privacy advice, and it applies to the model as much as to the chats. Confirming the chat set was deleted, option B, is the runner-up: deletion removes the source, not what the model learned from it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model files deserve protection. But encryption controls who can read the files, not whether the chats inside the model may serve marketing.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because deleting source data is a sound retirement step. But the model still carries what it memorized, so the reuse question remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a new use needs a fitness check. But good campaign copy does not settle whether customers' chats may be reused for marketing.

tips: Eliminate: A protects the files without settling whether the reuse is allowed, and C tests writing quality, not whether customers' chats may serve marketing.
Final two: D beats B because the model keeps what it memorized after the chats are deleted; reusing it for marketing needs the data owner's decision.
Exam cue: a model trained on personal data carries that data's purpose limits; reusing the model needs the same decision as reusing the data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); NIST AI 100-2e2025 Section 3.3.2 (Information Extraction)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.3 Retention, Deletion and Model Memorization (models can memorize training examples, so retired models and their files are disposed of like the personal data they learned from). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 3, 31 Oct 2026. Cross-domain gate fix, 31 Oct 2026: reusing a model fine-tuned on personal data for a new purpose.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Widening a summarizer's risk assessment
questions.question: A Norwegian patent office follows the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, yet its generative filing-summary assistant's risk assessment lists only accuracy and drift. Which source should the IS auditor recommend as BEST for widening it?

options.A: The vendor's model card listing the model's benchmark test results
options.B: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework used as the security baseline
options.C: The EU AI Act's list of banned AI practices
options.D: The twelve risks set out in NIST AI 600-1

questions.key_concept: The NIST Generative AI Profile extends the AI RMF to generative AI risks, such as confabulation and information integrity, that predictive-style assessments miss.
questions.pre_read: Read what the assessment lists and what the assistant does before weighing each source.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile applies the AI RMF to generative AI and describes risks a predictive-style assessment misses, such as confabulation, information integrity and intellectual property, all relevant to summaries of patent filings. The vendor's model card, option A, is the runner-up: its benchmark results are scores on tests the vendor chose, not a structured set of risks to check the assessment against.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model cards document a model's tested limits. But benchmark results are scores on tests the vendor chose, not a set of risks to widen the assessment against.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because NIST frameworks work together. But the Cybersecurity Framework organizes security outcomes, not risks such as invented facts in summaries.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI law sets firm limits. But banned practices mark uses that are prohibited outright; they do not list the risks of a lawful summarizing assistant.

tips: Eliminate: C lists banned practices, not the risks of a lawful assistant, and B organizes cybersecurity outcomes, not risks such as invented facts.
Final two: D beats A because the profile is a structured set of generative AI risks to check the assessment against; benchmark results are scores on tests the vendor chose.
Exam cue: for generative AI, widen risk work with the NIST Generative AI Profile; risks such as confabulation fall outside predictive-model checks.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.8 (Information Integrity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (a companion NIST profile applies the AI RMF to generative AI and describes risks such as confabulation). questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Targeting workplace inspections
questions.question: A South African labor inspectorate's model ranks workplaces for inspection; it is trained on past inspections, labeled by violations found, at sites inspectors chose to visit. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain the model on more years of the same past inspections
options.B: Have the owner add randomly chosen sites to each year's inspections
options.C: Rank sites by their past violation counts instead of using the model
options.D: Have inspectors record violations to one standard in every region

questions.key_concept: Labels that exist only for cases people chose to check teach a model their past choices; unselected cases must be checked to learn the rest.
questions.pre_read: Read how the training data was produced before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: The model only knows sites inspectors already chose to visit, so kinds of workplaces they rarely visited have no violation labels and stay ranked low, which keeps inspectors away from them. Inspecting some randomly chosen sites each year gives labels for parts of the population the old choices never reached. Standard recording of violations, option D, improves label quality, but only for sites that were visited.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more data often helps. But more years of the same choices repeat the same blind spot rather than filling it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems simpler and transparent. But past violation counts come from the same chosen visits, so the ranking inherits the same gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because inconsistent labels weaken a model. But better recording still covers only sites inspectors chose, so the unvisited kinds of workplace stay invisible.

tips: Eliminate: A adds more of the same chosen visits, repeating the blind spot, and C swaps the model for counts drawn from those same visits.
Final two: B beats D because only sites never chosen lack labels; better recording improves labels already collected but adds none for unvisited sites.
Exam cue: when labels exist only where people looked, the model learns where people looked; ask how the cases nobody checked get checked.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1A.2 How Models Learn and Where They Fail (a model learns from its labels; labels that exist only where people chose to look teach it their past choices). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Building a model in-house
questions.question: An Ecuadorian volcano observatory's business case funds a contract team to build an eruption-warning model over 18 months; it funds nothing after launch. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Newer modeling methods may make the model look dated within a year
options.B: The in-house model may prove less accurate than vendor products
options.C: Its accuracy could fade unnoticed as seismic patterns shift
options.D: Open-source modeling libraries may carry unmet license obligations

questions.key_concept: A model is not finished at launch: the data it meets keep changing, so building one needs funded owners who monitor, revalidate and retrain it.
questions.pre_read: Note what the business case pays for and what it does not, then rank each risk by realistic harm to the people relying on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Unlike fixed software, a model's accuracy depends on the data it meets, and a volcano's seismic patterns can shift over time. With nothing funded after launch, no one is paid to monitor or retrain the model, so accuracy could fade unnoticed in a life-safety system. Accuracy against vendor products, option B, matters at selection, but even the best model at launch needs upkeep.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI methods change fast. But looking dated is about novelty, not harm; the risk that matters is warnings degrading while nobody watches.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because build-or-buy choices weigh accuracy. But even a model that starts best can degrade; the business case leaves its upkeep unfunded.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because in-house builds often use open-source code. But license terms are a manageable legal check; they do not threaten whether eruption warnings stay reliable.

tips: Eliminate: D raises a manageable licensing check rather than a threat to the warnings, and A weighs novelty rather than harm.
Final two: C beats B because any model can degrade as conditions change; with no one watching, accuracy could fade unnoticed, whatever it starts at.
Exam cue: when building or buying AI, check the plan funds monitoring and retraining for the model's life, not just the build.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 2.2 (Mechanisms sustain the value of deployed AI); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Agents built by staff
questions.question: A Belgian chocolate maker's AI policy covers only models IT builds or buys; staff's agents, built in a no-code tool, send email and edit shared files. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Agent emails may vary in tone from those staff write
options.B: IT has set no write limits on the agents' file access
options.C: The tool's license may not cover every employee who builds
options.D: Agents act on company data with no owner or risk review

questions.key_concept: AI governance covers AI however it is made: agents staff build in everyday tools need the same policy, inventory and risk review as bought models.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the policy's scope matches every way AI now enters the organization, including tools staff configure themselves.
questions.correct_explanation: Agents that send email and edit shared files act on company data, yet a policy limited to IT-built or bought models leaves them uninventoried, unowned and unassessed, so nobody knows which exist or what they can do. Bringing them under policy and inventory comes first. Missing write limits, option B, is a real exposure, but limits can only be set well once each agent is known, owned and rated by risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generated messages can sound off-brand. But tone is a quality issue; agents acting on data with no owner or review can do real harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because agents that edit files need limits. But limits are set well only once each agent is known, owned and rated; unknown agents stay unassessed whatever IT restricts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because license terms matter. But license coverage is a contract question; the larger risk is agents acting on company data unreviewed.

tips: Eliminate: A raises message tone, a quality issue, and C a license question; neither is the risk of agents acting unreviewed.
Final two: D beats B because governance comes first: missing write limits are one symptom, and limits can be set by risk only once each agent is inventoried and owned.
Exam cue: when AI enters through everyday tools, widen policy and inventory first; technical limits follow from knowing what exists.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.6 (Mechanisms to inventory AI systems); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-11 (User-Installed Software)

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Requests for audit to approve
questions.question: A Slovenian car-leasing firm's credit model pauses itself when drift passes a limit; the firm wants internal audit, which audited the alert, to approve each restart. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner decide each restart against set criteria
options.B: Have the data scientists who built the model approve each restart
options.C: Let the model restart itself once its drift score returns to normal
options.D: Have internal audit approve each restart after reviewing retraining evidence

questions.key_concept: Deciding when a paused model returns belongs to its owner; internal audit assesses that control and never runs or approves it.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing who approves, ask whose decision a restart is and what internal audit would later have to assess.
questions.correct_explanation: Pausing and restarting a credit model are operating decisions with consequences for applicants and the firm, so they belong to the model owner, deciding against criteria set in advance. Internal audit can then assess whether the pause rule and restart decisions work. Internal audit approving restarts after reviewing retraining evidence, option D, sounds rigorous, but it makes internal audit part of the control it must later assess.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because builders know the model best. But builders approving their own model's return lacks independent challenge; the business owner answers for the decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it removes delay. But a drift score returning to normal does not show the model's errors were fixed, and no accountable person decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because internal audit knows the alert and would review evidence first. But approving restarts makes it part of the control it must assess, impairing its independence.

tips: Eliminate: C lets a drift score decide without an accountable person, and B has the builders approve their own model's return without independent challenge.
Final two: A beats D because restarts are the owner's operating decisions; internal audit approving them, however carefully, would mean auditing its own work.
Exam cue: when asked to approve, sign or run an AI control, the IS auditor recommends that the owner take it on and remains the assessor.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Override rates and officer training
questions.question: A Nepali land-revenue office's AI program reports that all valuation officers finished training on questioning model output; officers overrode 3 of 40,000 model valuations last year. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team retest valuation accuracy each quarter
options.B: Repeat the training for the officers with the fewest overrides
options.C: Set a minimum number of overrides for every officer
options.D: Add a measure of whether officers catch seeded wrong valuations

questions.key_concept: Training completion shows activity, not oversight; measure whether reviewers actually catch the model's errors, for example with seeded test cases.
questions.pre_read: Read what the program reports and the override figure before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: Three overrides in 40,000 could mean an excellent model or officers accepting valuations without real review, and training completion cannot tell the two apart. Seeding known-wrong valuations and measuring how many officers catch them shows whether oversight works and where training is not taking hold. Repeating training for officers with the fewest overrides, option B, assumes both the problem and its location before anyone knows whether review fails.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model accuracy matters. But it measures the model, not the officers; the program's training claim needs a direct measure of whether officers catch wrong valuations.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because training may not have stuck. But it treats few overrides as proof of weak review, which nobody has shown; the program first needs a measure of review quality.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because overrides seem healthy. But quotas push officers to disagree for the sake of it, producing worse decisions rather than real review.

tips: Eliminate: C sets a quota that forces disagreement rather than judgment, and A measures the model rather than whether officers catch its errors.
Final two: D beats B because seeded cases show whether officers catch errors; retraining low overriders assumes an answer the metrics cannot yet give.
Exam cue: program metrics should show whether human oversight catches AI errors, not just that people were trained.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 1.2 (Metrics and control effectiveness regularly assessed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 3.5 (Processes for human oversight defined and assessed)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Sources for identifying AI risk
questions.question: A Ugandan teachers' commission's model, trained on past transfers, ranks teachers for remote postings; its risk register holds only risks raised by IT, legal and data scientists. Which gap should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Harms seen by teachers and principals may be missing
options.B: Teachers' transfer risks may not be scored on one common scale
options.C: The register omits patch status for the model's servers
options.D: The register lacks the model vendor's accuracy benchmark

questions.key_concept: Identifying AI risk needs the people the model affects and those who work with it; internal technical teams alone miss harms only those people see.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would notice first if the ranking treated someone unfairly, and whether they were asked.
questions.correct_explanation: A model trained on past transfers can repeat whatever patterns shaped them, such as who was sent far from family, and apply them to every teacher at once. Those harms are visible to teachers and principals, not to IT, legal or data scientists, so a register built without them may miss the risks that matter most. Scoring on a common scale, option B, improves assessment, but it cannot rate risks nobody identified.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consistent scoring is good practice. But scoring works only on risks already identified; harms only teachers would raise are still missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because server security matters. But treating AI risk as a security question misses the harm wrong rankings do to teachers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks inform likelihood. But a vendor benchmark is an input to assessment, not a source of the harms the register lacks.

tips: Eliminate: C treats AI risk as a server security matter, and D adds a vendor benchmark, which informs assessment but identifies no harms.
Final two: A beats B because a register can only score risks someone raised; without the people affected, the harms that matter may never appear.
Exam cue: AI risk identification draws on the people affected and the staff who use the system, not only technical and legal teams.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Indicators for AI errors
questions.question: A Nigerian payment switch's monthly-average key risk indicator (KRI) for wrongly blocked payments stayed within tolerance, though a vendor model update tripled wrong blocks for four days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Count breaches when complaints pass the monthly limit
options.B: Have the vendor confirm each update stayed within tolerance
options.C: Track the indicator daily and by model version against tolerance
options.D: Lower the monthly threshold so smaller rises count as breaches

questions.key_concept: AI KRIs must be measured at a grain that shows harm after changes; averaging over a month can hide a model update's short, sharp spike.
questions.pre_read: Read how the indicator is calculated and what happened before weighing each recommendation.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor update can change a model's behavior overnight, so harm arrives as spikes tied to versions, which a monthly average dilutes. Measuring daily and by model version shows each update's effect against tolerance and triggers escalation while customers are still affected. Lowering the monthly threshold, option D, makes the average more sensitive, but a short spike is still averaged away and still not tied to the update.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because complaints show customer harm. But complaints lag and undercount, so tying breaches to them hides harm the switch's own data already shows.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor made the update. But that replaces the switch's own measurement with the vendor's claim about its own update.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tighter thresholds catch smaller rises. But the window is the problem: a four-day spike is still diluted across the month, whatever the threshold.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's claim about its own update, and A ties breaches to complaints, which lag and undercount the harm.
Final two: C beats D because the monthly window hides short spikes whatever the threshold; daily, versioned tracking ties harm to the update that caused it.
Exam cue: set AI KRIs at the grain where changes happen, such as each model version, so a bad update shows before the month ends.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.4 (Functionality and behavior monitored in production); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1C.2 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and AI Key Risk Indicators (AI KRIs need thresholds and a measurement grain that show breaches of tolerance, including after each model change). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 5, 5 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Controlling data used for training
questions.question: A New Zealand health insurer's data team may train models on any of 300 platform datasets it can access. Which control should the IS auditor consider BEST against training on data not cleared for it?

options.A: Owner-set tags of permitted uses, checked before each training run
options.B: Encryption of every dataset stored on the platform
options.C: Access rules limiting the data team to tables marked non-sensitive
options.D: Annual privacy and data-handling training for everyone on the data team

questions.key_concept: Rights to use data for training depend on purpose and terms, not sensitivity alone; owners record permitted uses so pipelines can check before training.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions: who may see a dataset, and what it may be used for.
questions.correct_explanation: Whether a dataset may train a model depends on its terms and purpose, such as consent, license or the reason it was collected, which its data owner decides. Tags recording each dataset's permitted uses, checked before training starts, turn those decisions into a preventive control. Limiting the team to non-sensitive tables, option C, controls who sees data, not what it may be used for: licensed or purpose-bound data can be non-sensitive.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects data. But the data team can still read and train on encrypted data it can access, so encryption does not limit use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because least privilege is a strong control. But sensitivity is not purpose; non-sensitive licensed or purpose-bound data may still be barred from training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training shapes behavior. But it relies on memory and cannot tell a data scientist which of 300 datasets are cleared for training.

tips: Eliminate: B protects data from outsiders but not from use by the team, and D relies on memory rather than a check of each dataset's terms.
Final two: A beats C because rights to use depend on purpose and terms, not sensitivity; access rules decide who sees data, not what trains models.
Exam cue: for training data, look for a control that records and checks each dataset's permitted uses before the model is built.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-07 (Inventories of data and metadata maintained); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1D.1 Data Governance for AI (rights to use data for training are decided by data owners and recorded, so pipelines can check them before training). questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Planning with the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: An Argentine provincial road-safety agency will use the NIST AI RMF to rank improvements across its twelve AI uses, seven of them generative. Which approach should the IS auditor consider BEST aligned with the framework?

options.A: Apply the Generative AI Profile's actions to the seven generative uses
options.B: Compare current and target profiles, then plan to close the gaps
options.C: Adopt the framework as mandatory regulation for its twelve AI uses
options.D: Plan improvements for the newest AI uses before older ones

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF uses profiles: comparing a current profile with a target profile shows gaps, and closing them is prioritized by risk.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem's facts about the agency's plan before weighing each approach.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF describes current and target profiles: a current profile shows how AI risk is managed today, a target profile the outcomes needed, and comparing them reveals gaps for action plans prioritized by risk and resources. Applying the Generative AI Profile to the seven generative uses, option A, confuses NIST's cross-sectoral profile for generative AI with the current and target profiles that show this agency's own gaps.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because NIST AI 600-1 profiles generative AI. But it covers only seven uses and lists cross-sector actions; it shows neither where each use stands nor which gaps come first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because frameworks feel authoritative. But the NIST AI RMF is voluntary; the agency may adopt it, but that does not make it regulation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because new AI uses feel riskiest. But the framework orders gaps by risk and resources; novelty alone shows neither where harm is likely nor current gaps.

tips: Eliminate: D orders the work by novelty rather than risk, and C treats a voluntary framework as regulation.

Final two: B beats A because current and target profiles show this agency's own gaps to close by priority; the Generative AI Profile lists generative AI risks and suggested actions, not a gap analysis.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, current and target profiles turn the framework into a prioritized, risk-based plan.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 6 (AI RMF Profiles); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 1.2 (Treatment prioritized by impact, likelihood and resources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.3 Frameworks and Standards for AI (the NIST AI RMF uses current and target profiles to find gaps and plan improvements by priority). Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. The Govern function
questions.question: A Japanese trading house finished its NIST AI RMF Govern work in 2024 and now applies only Map, Measure and Manage to each new model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have management treat Govern as complete, since policies were approved
options.B: Have the IS auditor refresh the AI policy every year
options.C: Have model owners update risk tolerances when mapping each model
options.D: Have senior management review Govern outcomes as AI uses change

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, Govern is cross-cutting and ongoing: its policies, roles and tolerances need periodic review as AI uses change.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether governance set two years ago still fits the models adopted since.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF calls Govern cross-cutting, infused throughout the other functions, and calls attention to governance a continual requirement over an AI system's lifespan. Policies, roles and tolerances set in 2024 may not fit models adopted since, so senior management should review Govern outcomes as uses change. Having model owners update tolerances while mapping each model, option C, hands senior management's tolerances to owners and leaves the 2024 policies and roles unreviewed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the policies were approved. But Govern is cross-cutting and ongoing; policies set in 2024 need review as new AI uses arrive.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit sees where governance falls short. But writing policy is management's job; audit assesses the policy and would lose independence by maintaining it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the Map function documents risk tolerances. But senior management sets them; owners adjusting tolerances model by model leave the 2024 policies and roles unreviewed.

tips: Eliminate: A treats Govern as a one-time project, and B has the IS auditor maintain policy that audit must assess.
Final two: D beats C because Govern is ongoing and tolerances are senior management's; owners adjusting them model by model leave the 2024 policies and roles unreviewed.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, Govern is cross-cutting and continuing; look for periodic review of policies, roles and tolerances, not a finished project.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 5.1 (Govern is a cross-cutting function infused throughout the others); NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.5 (Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Agents replacing scripted bots
questions.question: A Jordanian water utility's AI agent, planning its own steps, replaced a scripted billing-dispute bot and passed the bot's test scripts; system-enforced credit limits remain. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent's dispute decisions may be harder to explain than the bot's
options.B: No test shows the agent learned from the bot's past billing disputes
options.C: Passing the bot's tests cannot show how the agent will behave
options.D: The agent may grant credits above the system-enforced limits

questions.key_concept: A scripted bot follows fixed steps; an agent chooses its steps at run time, so passing the bot's scripts shows little about the agent.
questions.pre_read: Compare how the old and the new system decide a dispute before weighing each risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The bot's test scripts check fixed steps on fixed cases, which suited a bot that always followed them. An agent plans its steps at run time, so passing those scripts shows only how it handled those cases, not the paths it may choose on others; it must be tested as deployed. Harder-to-explain decisions, option A, are a real agent concern, but explainability is one property such testing would assess.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agents are harder to trace than scripts. But that is one property to assess; the gap is that no test reflects how the agent now works.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models learn from data. But training on past disputes would not show how the agent behaves as deployed; only testing the agent itself does.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because agents can overreach. But limits enforced by the billing system hold whatever the agent plans, so they are not the main concern here.

tips: Eliminate: B treats training on past disputes as evidence of behavior, and D forgets that system-enforced limits bind whatever the agent plans.
Final two: C beats A because scripts with fixed steps cannot show the paths an agent chooses at run time; explainability is one property that testing the agent as deployed would assess.
Exam cue: when a scripted bot becomes an agent, passing the old scripts proves little; the agent must be tested as it now works.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.1 (Tasks and methods the AI system supports are defined)

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Tolerances for a benefits chatbot
questions.question: An Estonian unemployment fund's board has low appetite for claimants acting on wrong guidance; the tolerance for its benefits chatbot is average user satisfaction of 4 of 5. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: An average of 4 of 5 is too low a target
options.B: Claimants may rate fluent but incorrect answers highly
options.C: The board, not senior management, should set the tolerance
options.D: Satisfaction ratings come from a small share of claimants

questions.key_concept: A tolerance must measure the harm the appetite names; generative answers can satisfy users while being wrong, so satisfaction cannot stand in for accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the appetite names with what the tolerance measures.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance should measure the harm the appetite names: claimants acting on wrong guidance. Generative chatbots give fluent, confident answers, so users often rate wrong answers highly; satisfaction can stay high while errors rise. The tolerance needs a measure of answer accuracy, such as sampled answers checked against benefit rules. Few raters, option D, weakens the measure, but a full response rate would still measure the wrong thing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a higher bar sounds safer. But raising a satisfaction target still does not measure wrong guidance, the harm the board named.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the board owns appetite. But the board need not set tolerances itself; senior management often sets them within appetite, and who set this one is not the problem.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because low response rates bias surveys. But even if every claimant rated, satisfaction would not show whether the guidance was right.

tips: Eliminate: C treats who set the tolerance as the flaw, though senior management may set it within appetite, and A tightens a measure that cannot detect wrong guidance.
Final two: B beats D because the measure itself misses the named harm; fixing the survey's coverage would still measure satisfaction, not accuracy.
Exam cue: a tolerance must measure the harm the appetite names; user satisfaction does not show whether AI answers are correct.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements established); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation)
