questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Reliability criteria for a shortlisting model
questions.question: Using the NIST AI RMF, a Rwandan urban-resettlement agency judges its household-shortlisting model reliable by one criterion: 99.95% monthly uptime of its hosting platform. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner add a disaster-recovery test to the criterion
options.B: Have the model owner raise the uptime target to 99.99% monthly
options.C: Have the model owner add a criterion on correct outputs over time
options.D: Have the model owner add an ongoing criterion on group fairness parity

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, reliable means performing as required, without failure, over time and in use; platform uptime does not measure it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the current criterion actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: In the NIST AI RMF, reliable means the system performs as required, without failure, over time and under its conditions of use. Uptime shows that the platform answers, not that its shortlists are right. Fairness parity, option D, is a separate RMF characteristic: groups can be treated alike while shortlists are wrong for all of them, so the criterion must measure correct shortlists over time.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recovery tests strengthen resilience. But they still measure the platform, not whether households are shortlisted correctly.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a higher target sounds more reliable. But any uptime figure shows the platform answers, not that its shortlists are right.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it tracks the model's outputs over time. But fairness is a separate RMF characteristic; parity across groups can hold while shortlists are wrong for every group.

tips: Eliminate: B and A both measure the hosting platform, which says nothing about whether households are shortlisted correctly.
Final two: C beats D because the RMF's reliable means performing as required over time; fairness is a separate characteristic, and parity can hold while every shortlist is wrong.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, reliable means performing as required over time in real use; uptime and other characteristics, such as fairness, do not show it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.1 (Valid and Reliable); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1E.1 Trustworthy-AI Characteristics as Testable Criteria (each characteristic becomes a measurable criterion; in the NIST AI RMF, reliable means performing as required over time in use, which platform uptime does not measure). Round 1 review: reworked to a new angle, as the fairness-after-human-changes frame repeated aaia_d2_204. Round 3: key reworded to 'correct outputs' so no stem word is echoed only in the key; principle tag removed, as the RMF meaning of reliable versus fair (knowledge) decides, like aaia_d1_046. Original scenario and wording; no ISACA review manual, QAE, online course or prep-bank text used. AAIA batch 7, 12 Nov 2026.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. The committee's role after launch
questions.question: An Uzbek fertilizer producer's AI governance committee approves high-impact models before launch; afterwards, only the data team reads the models' monitoring reports. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the committee re-approve each model when a change is submitted
options.B: Have the data team retrain any model whose reports show drift
options.C: Have model owners get monitoring results and escalate breaches
options.D: Have internal audit review every model's monitoring reports monthly

questions.key_concept: Approval at launch is not lifelong oversight; monitoring results should reach each model's accountable owner, who escalates breaches to the committee.
questions.pre_read: Follow the model's life after approval before weighing each option.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's behavior can shift in any week as its data drifts, with no change anyone submits for approval, so oversight after launch has to run on monitoring. Sending results to each accountable owner, with breaches escalated to the committee, puts decisions with people who can act. Re-approval when a change is submitted, option A, covers retrains and updates, but drift submits nothing, so it would pass unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because changes need approval. But drift can push a model past its limits with no change submitted, so change-triggered review leaves owners blind in between.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining treats drift. But the data team would change high-impact models with no owner deciding, which is the gap, not the remedy.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit is independent. But reviewing monitoring is management's oversight duty; audit doing it monthly would take over a control it must later assess.

tips: Eliminate: D gives internal audit a management monitoring duty it must stay independent of, and B lets builders change models with no accountable owner deciding.
Final two: C beats A because drift can arrive any week without a submitted change, so owners need monitoring results, not only change-triggered re-approval.
Exam cue: approval at launch is not oversight for life; look for monitoring results that reach an owner who can act and escalate.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 2.1 (Roles, responsibilities and lines of communication documented); NIST AI 100-1 MANAGE 4.1 (Post-deployment monitoring including appeal, override, incident response and change management)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Controls mapped to explanation duties
questions.question: An AI law gives jobseekers profiled by a Portuguese employment service's model a right to an explanation; its obligations register maps that duty to the vendor's model card. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The card explains the model overall, not any one jobseeker's result
options.B: The duty falls on the model's vendor, not the employment service
options.C: The card is written for data specialists, not for jobseekers
options.D: Caseworkers make final decisions, so jobseekers need no explanation

questions.key_concept: An explanation duty is met per decision; a model card describes the model in general, so it cannot explain any one person's result.
questions.pre_read: Read the duty and the mapped control side by side.
questions.correct_explanation: A right to an explanation concerns each person's decision: which factors drove that jobseeker's profile. A model card describes the model in general, such as its purpose, data, overall performance and main factors on average, so the mapped control cannot meet the duty for anyone. A plain-language card, option C, would be easier to read, but it would still explain no single profile.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors build the model. But risk-based laws give organizations using high-risk AI their own duties toward the people affected.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because explanations must be understandable. But even a plain-language card describes the model in general; it never explains why a given jobseeker got their profile.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a person decides. But a caseworker's final say does not remove the duty, and the model's output still shapes each decision.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes only the vendor has duties, though users of high-risk AI have their own, and D assumes a person's final say removes the duty to explain.
Final two: A beats C because a model card explains the model in general, however plainly written, while the duty asks why each jobseeker got their result.
Exam cue: when mapping a duty to a control, check the control delivers what the duty asks, at the level it asks: one person's decision, not the model overall.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Cybersecurity frameworks and AI risk
questions.question: An Omani driving-test center is told its NIST CSF 2.0 profile, at Tier 3, covers the risks of its model scoring candidates' driving tests. Which gap should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Tier 3 is below the Tier 4 that regulators require
options.B: The profile addresses cybersecurity, not the outputs' validity or bias
options.C: CSF 2.0 profiles must be certified before test centers rely on them
options.D: Tier 3 describes how practices are managed, not whether controls operate

questions.key_concept: Cybersecurity frameworks cover security outcomes; an AI model's validity, harmful bias and explainability need AI-specific criteria such as the NIST AI RMF.
questions.pre_read: Read the claim made in the stem and decide what evidence it would need.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 covers security outcomes such as protecting, detecting and recovering. A scoring model's main risks lie elsewhere: whether its scores are valid, whether it treats candidates fairly and whether people can explain and challenge it, which the NIST AI RMF addresses. A Tier 3 rating, option D, describes how rigorously practices are managed, but even a strong security profile leaves those AI risks unassessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tiers sound like grades. But tiers describe how rigorously risk is managed; the framework does not set a tier that regulators require.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certificates reassure test centers. But CSF 2.0 is voluntary guidance with no certification scheme; organizations rely on assessed outcomes, not certificates.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tiers do not prove controls work. But even proven security controls would leave the model's validity and fairness unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a voluntary framework as needing certification, and A reads tiers as required grades, which the framework does not set.
Final two: B beats D because a perfectly operating security profile still leaves validity and fairness untested, while tier rigor is a lesser question.
Exam cue: match the framework to the risk; cybersecurity frameworks cover security, while AI risks such as bias need AI-specific criteria.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Safeguards supplied by a model provider
questions.question: A Slovenian foraging app's chatbot tells users which wild mushrooms are safe to eat; it relies only on its model provider's built-in safety filters for harmful content. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The provider may change its filters without telling the app
options.B: Unsafe mushroom advice may pass filters made for general use
options.C: Filters may block too many harmless questions about mushrooms
options.D: The provider is liable for harmful advice its filters let through

questions.key_concept: Provider filters target general harms; harms specific to one use, such as unsafe foraging advice, need the deployer's own controls and tests.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: A provider's built-in filters are designed for harms common to all customers, such as violence or hate speech. Advice calling a poisonous mushroom edible reads as ordinary text and passes them easily, so the app needs its own use-specific controls and testing. Silent filter changes, option A, are a real third-party risk, but even unchanged filters were never built to catch unsafe foraging advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because providers do change hosted components quietly. But even unchanged filters were built for general harms and would still pass unsafe foraging advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because over-blocking frustrates users. But blocked questions are visible and inconvenient, while unsafe advice that passes can poison users unseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the provider supplies the filters. But the app chose to advise on wild mushrooms and stays accountable for it; a contract cannot shift that.

tips: Eliminate: D shifts accountability to the provider, which the app keeps, and C weighs inconvenience above the risk of poisoning users.
Final two: B beats A because even unchanged general-purpose filters would pass advice that is harmful only in this use.
Exam cue: a provider's safeguards cover general risks; the organization deploying the model owns the risks of its own use.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Documents an assistant retrieves
questions.question: A Guatemalan hospital group's AI assistant for nurses, used via each hospital's sign-in, searches one index of its four hospitals' current care protocols, which differ on some doses. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Answers may quote dose tables that have since been replaced
options.B: Nurses may trust the assistant's drug answers over the protocols
options.C: The index may show one hospital's protocols to other hospitals' staff
options.D: Nurses may be given another hospital's dose for the same drug

questions.key_concept: Retrieval matches passages by similarity, not by where they apply, so documents pooled from several sites need owner-set records of where each applies.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: A hospital sign-in controls who uses the assistant, not which passages it retrieves, unless each protocol records where it applies and retrieval filters on it. Four hospitals' protocols for one drug match a question almost equally well, so a nurse can get another site's dose with no sign it is wrong. Staff seeing other sites' protocols, option C, stems from the same gap, but only a wrong dose harms a patient.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because outdated documents are a common retrieval risk. But the index pools current protocols; the stated difference is between hospitals, not versions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because over-reliance is a real oversight concern. But the facts give no sign of it, and the harm here comes from which protocol is retrieved.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because one index behind separate sign-ins looks like an access-control gap. But staff seeing a sister hospital's protocol matters far less than a wrong dose reaching a patient.

tips: Eliminate: A raises replaced dose tables when the index holds current protocols, and B assumes over-reliance the facts never give.
Final two: D beats C because both follow from a sign-in that does not scope similarity search, but only a wrong dose can harm a patient.
Exam cue: when one assistant searches documents from several owners or sites, ask whether each document records where it applies.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An assistant for kitchen managers
questions.question: A Uruguayan restaurant chain's kitchen managers ask its generative assistant, which searches current food-hygiene rules, to confirm storage practices they already plan to use. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Answers may lean toward whatever each question seems to expect
options.B: Its answers may be identical each time, hiding any error
options.C: Each confirmation may teach the assistant to approve more practices
options.D: Answers may rest on hygiene rules changed after its training cutoff

questions.key_concept: Models tuned on human approval can favor answers users seem to want, so leading questions draw agreement rather than an independent check.
questions.pre_read: Note which facts in the stem each option depends on before ranking them.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative models are tuned partly on human ratings, which tend to reward agreeable answers, so a request to confirm a planned practice can draw a yes that the rules do not support. Managers then get their own view back as advice. A training cutoff, option D, could date answers, but this assistant searches current rules; questions built to invite agreement are the gap the stem describes.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because uniform answers could hide a fault. But generative answers usually vary between runs, and nothing in the stem suggests identical replies.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI seems to learn from use. But answering a prompt does not retrain the model, so confirmations do not shift later answers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because models do miss rules made after their training. But this assistant searches current rules, while questions built to invite a yes can still draw one.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes each answer retrains the model, and B expects identical replies from a model whose answers usually vary between runs.
Final two: A beats D because the assistant searches current rules, yet questions framed to invite a yes still draw one from models tuned on human approval.
Exam cue: when users ask an AI to confirm their own view, expect agreement, not a check; neutral questions and source checks are the control.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Forecasts behind work stoppages
questions.question: A Greek labor inspectorate halts outdoor building work only when its model's forecast afternoon temperature exceeds 40°C; tomorrow's forecast is 38.5°C. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Work may be halted more often than it is needed
options.B: The single figure may hide a real chance of passing 40°C
options.C: Updated forecasts may differ from the one issued today
options.D: The forecast model may not have been tested on recent heatwaves

questions.key_concept: A model's forecast is an estimate with a spread; deciding on its single figure ignores the chance that the true value crosses the limit.
questions.pre_read: Restate the decision rule in your own words before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Forecasts are estimates: a central value of 38.5°C can still leave a sizable chance that the afternoon passes 40°C, yet the rule treats it as no risk at all. Decisions where the harm is heatstroke need the forecast's range or its probability of crossing the limit. Testing on recent heatwaves, option D, would refine the estimate, but even a well-validated forecast is a range, not a promise.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because needless stoppages carry costs. But this rule halts work only above 40°C, so missed dangerous heat, not excess stoppages, is its weak side.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because changing forecasts look unreliable. But updating as new weather data arrive is normal and useful, not a flaw.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because validation on recent seasons is good practice. But a well-tested model still gives an estimate with a spread, and the rule ignores that spread.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about too many stoppages under a rule that triggers only above the limit, and C treats normal forecast updates as a defect.
Final two: B beats D because even a validated forecast is an estimate with a spread; deciding on its single figure ignores the chance of passing 40°C.
Exam cue: when a decision compares a model's single figure with a hard limit, ask for the chance of crossing the limit, not just the central estimate.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A model tuned for another team
questions.question: A Saudi telecom's legal team fine-tuned the HR department's policy-answering model to draft supplier contracts; the AI inventory lists the HR director as owner of both models. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the AI governance committee own both models jointly
options.B: Have the data team own both models, since it maintains them
options.C: Have the HR director extend validation to drafting contracts
options.D: Have the leader who answers for contracts own the tuned copy

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning creates a new model for a new use; ownership follows the use, so the leader answering for that work owns the tuned model.
questions.pre_read: Separate what changed in the system from what stayed the same.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning made a new model with new behavior for a new use, drafting supplier contracts, which the HR director neither answers for nor is placed to judge. Ownership follows the use, so the leader who answers for contract work should own the tuned model and accept it. Extending validation, option C, is needed, but run by the HR director it leaves contract risk owned by someone who answers only for HR policy.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because committees oversee AI. But a committee sets standards and approves uses; each model needs one named owner who answers for it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the data team knows the models best. But building and maintaining a model does not make anyone accountable for its business decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the tuned model does need validating. But under the HR director, contract-drafting risk stays owned by someone who answers only for HR policy.

tips: Eliminate: B makes the builders owners, and A gives ownership to a committee; each model needs one named business owner.
Final two: D beats C because the tuned model serves contract drafting, so its owner is the leader who answers for that work, not the owner of the model it came from.
Exam cue: when a model is copied, tuned or reused for a new purpose, look for an owner tied to the new use.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. AI-filled fields in a case system
questions.question: A Portuguese social-security office's AI policy requires officers to check AI output; a new case-system feature fills household fields from scanned letters, shown exactly like typed fields. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner mark AI-filled values on the case screen
options.B: Have the owner check a monthly sample of AI-filled fields
options.C: Have the vendor certify the feature's accuracy before further use
options.D: Have officers retype each household field from the letters

questions.key_concept: A rule to check AI output works only if staff can tell which output is AI's, so AI-filled values must be marked on screen.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option would change in practice.
questions.correct_explanation: Officers can only follow the checking rule if they can see which values the AI wrote, and the screen shows them like a colleague's entries. Marking AI-filled fields makes the policy duty workable at the point of use. Monthly sampling, option B, would measure the error rate, but officers would still decide cases on unmarked AI values every day.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because sampling measures how often the feature errs. But it finds errors after decisions are made, while officers still cannot tell which values to check.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendor evidence feels reassuring. But a certificate is an input, not assurance, and officers still could not see which values the AI wrote.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retyping removes AI errors. But it discards the feature instead of making the checking duty workable, and retyping adds its own errors.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on a vendor certificate, which is an input, not assurance, and D drops the feature rather than making the policy's check workable.
Final two: A beats B because officers can apply a checking duty only to output they can recognize; sampling measures errors after unmarked values have shaped decisions.
Exam cue: a rule to check AI output works only if people can tell which output is AI's.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Likelihood ratings for a multi-step agent
questions.question: A Paraguayan property manager rates its tenant-onboarding agent's error likelihood low, citing 95% accuracy on single steps tested alone with correct inputs; each onboarding takes about ten steps. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The 95% figure needs retesting by a team independent of builders
options.B: The rating holds, since about 95% of onboardings will be error-free
options.C: The rating holds once the agent learns from each onboarding error
options.D: The rating understates how often whole onboardings go wrong

questions.key_concept: Errors compound across an agent's steps: ten independent steps at 95% each leave about 60% of tasks fully right, so judge likelihood per task.
questions.pre_read: Restate the rating's claim in your own words before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Errors compound across an agent's steps: if each of ten steps were right 95% of the time and errors were independent, only about 60% of onboardings would come out fully right. Steps tested alone with correct inputs also never show one step's error feeding the next. The rating uses the wrong unit, a step instead of a task. An independent retest, option A, would only confirm the step figure.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independence improves evidence. But an independent retest would confirm the per-step figure, which still compounds to frequent errors across ten steps.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because 95% sounds like the task's success rate. But it is per step; across ten steps the chance of an error-free onboarding falls to about 60%.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI is assumed to learn as it works. But completing onboardings does not retrain the agent, and learning would not fix the rating's unit error.

tips: Eliminate: B reads a per-step rate as a per-onboarding rate, and C assumes the agent improves by working, which does not retrain it.
Final two: D beats A because step accuracy compounds across ten steps, to about 60% error-free if errors are independent; independent testing would confirm the step rate, not undo the compounding.
Exam cue: for multi-step agents, judge likelihood per completed task; step accuracy compounds across the chain.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 5.1 (Likelihood and magnitude of impacts characterized); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Tuning a coding assistant
questions.question: A Romanian software firm will fine-tune a coding assistant it sells on its repository history; earlier commits hold passwords and keys removed from current code but never changed. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The assistant may suggest those credentials to its users
options.B: Suggestions may follow coding styles the firm has since dropped
options.C: Suggestions may include code with known security flaws
options.D: Training may alter the passwords and keys in earlier commits

questions.key_concept: Secrets removed from current code but never changed stay live in history a model trains on, and models can memorize rare strings such as keys.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the stem states from what it leaves open.
questions.correct_explanation: Training on full history feeds the model every commit, including passwords and keys removed from current code but never changed, so they still work. Models can memorize rare strings like these and reproduce them when a prompt resembles their context, so customers' developers who never had repository access could be shown them. Flawed suggestions, option C, are a real risk, but the stem's stated fact is live secrets in the history.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because history holds practices the firm has dropped. But dated style is a quality nuisance; live credentials shown to outsiders are a security breach.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because coding assistants can suggest flawed code. But the stem points to unchanged secrets in commit history, which the model can memorize and hand out.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training touches the repository. But fine-tuning reads the history; it does not change commits or what they contain.

tips: Eliminate: D thinks training alters the repository, and B weighs dated coding style, a nuisance beside live credentials.
Final two: A beats C because keys removed but never changed still work, and a model trained on the history can memorize and repeat such rare strings.
Exam cue: secrets removed from code but never changed stay live in history; ask whether a model will train on that history.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.4 (Data Privacy); NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.9 (Information Security)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Safety criteria for a health chatbot
questions.question: A Tunisian health hotline's chatbot, tuned until red-team tests found zero unsafe medical answers, now refuses 40% of routine clinic-hours questions. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The chatbot meets its safety goal, as tests found no unsafe answers
options.B: The vendor should retune the chatbot and approve the result
options.C: Refusals are a usability issue outside the safety review
options.D: Needless refusals are themselves a risk to callers

questions.key_concept: Refusing safe, needed answers is a harm too; tuning a model hard toward one trustworthy-AI characteristic can cost the others.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Tuning only against unsafe answers can teach a model to refuse anything health-related, and a red-team score counts that as success. But a caller refused clinic hours may not get care, so the refusals are a harm that zero unsafe answers never measures. Treating the test result as meeting the safety goal, option A, counts only one side of the harm the tuning created.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because zero unsafe answers is strong test evidence. But it measures only one side; refusing routine questions harms callers the tests never counted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor can retune the model. But approving the result is the owner's decision, and the vendor would be approving its own work.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because refusals look like a convenience problem. But a caller refused clinic hours may not get care; harm from refusing belongs in the safety review.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the vendor approve its own fix, and C files refusals under usability, though refusing needed answers can harm callers.
Final two: D beats A because zero unsafe answers measures only one side of safety; refusing routine questions harms callers the tests never counted.
Exam cue: when an AI is tuned to one trustworthy-AI characteristic, ask what the tuning costs the others, including harm from refusing.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Explaining refusals with similar cases
questions.question: A Slovenian town's kindergarten-admission model explains each refusal by showing three similar accepted families' anonymized profiles: street, household size and parents' jobs. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Similar-case explanations may expose the model's exact formula
options.B: Refused families may use the profiles to game reapplications
options.C: Neighbors could recognize the families in the profiles shown
options.D: Showing families as examples may make decisions less accurate

questions.key_concept: Explanations that show similar real cases trade explainability against privacy, since the cases shown can identify other people.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Example-based explanations show real people. In one town, a street, household size and parents' jobs are often enough for neighbors to recognize a family, so each refusal letter can expose three other households' details. Explainability here trades against privacy. Gaming reapplications, option B, is a known risk of explanations, but these fields are hard to change honestly, while the exposure harms families outside the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because explanations reveal something about a model. But example-based explanations show past cases, not the model's internal formula.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because explanations can teach people to game a model. But street, household size and parents' jobs are hard to change honestly; exposing other families is the graver harm.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because extra features can seem costly. But showing examples leaves the model's decisions unchanged; it affects what is disclosed, not accuracy.

tips: Eliminate: A thinks showing similar cases discloses the model's formula, and D links showing examples to accuracy, which they do not change.
Final two: C beats B because the shown fields identify real neighbors in a small town; gaming needs features families can change, and these are hard to change honestly.
Exam cue: explanations that show similar real cases trade explainability against privacy; check what the examples reveal about others.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A human step in automated denials
questions.question: A Lithuanian rent-to-own retailer says data-protection rules on solely automated decisions do not reach its contract-refusal model, since a clerk approves each refusal; none has ever been changed. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The rules may bar rent-to-own retailers from using any AI model
options.B: The model's supplier, not the retailer, may answer for refusals
options.C: Clerks may not record a reason when they make no change
options.D: Sign-offs that never change outcomes may not count as human review

questions.key_concept: Rules on solely automated decisions look at substance; a human approval that never changes outcomes may not take a decision outside them.
questions.pre_read: Restate the stem's claim in your own words before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Rules on solely automated decisions look at substance: a person must have the authority, competence and information to weigh and change each outcome. Sign-offs that have never changed an outcome may count as no human review at all, so the retailer may owe applicants rights it believes do not apply. Recording reasons, option C, improves evidence, but reasons on rubber-stamped approvals do not make the review meaningful.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI laws can restrict uses. But such rules set conditions and rights for automated decisions; they do not ban rent-to-own retailers from using models.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models often come from suppliers. But the retailer makes the refusals and answers for them, whoever built the model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recorded reasons are good evidence. But reasons written for approvals that never change anything do not make the human role meaningful.

tips: Eliminate: A reads rules on automated decisions as a ban on models, and B moves accountability for refusals to a supplier.
Final two: D beats C because a review that never changes outcomes may not count as human involvement at all; recorded reasons only document a rubber stamp.
Exam cue: when an organization relies on a human step to avoid automated-decision rules, test whether that person really weighs and changes outcomes.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Threat models built on MITRE ATLAS
questions.question: A Peruvian bank's threat model for its fraud models covers every MITRE ATLAS technique, so its owner records the threat model as complete. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: New techniques outside the catalog may go unassessed
options.B: The bank may need certification against the ATLAS standard
options.C: Listed techniques may be rated without the bank's own likelihood
options.D: ATLAS coverage may count as compliance with the NIST AI RMF

questions.key_concept: MITRE ATLAS is a growing knowledge base of observed attacks on AI, with mitigations; it guides threat modeling and testing but is never complete.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against the facts in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI, built from real attacks and research, and it grows as new ones appear. Recording the threat model as complete on that basis leaves the bank blind to attacks that are new or not yet cataloged. Rating listed techniques by the bank's own likelihood, option C, sharpens the model but cannot reach attacks the catalog does not yet hold.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ATLAS is widely cited. But it is a voluntary knowledge base, not a standard anyone certifies against.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because likelihood should reflect the bank's own setting. But better ratings of listed techniques still leave out every attack the catalog does not yet hold.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because both concern AI risk. But ATLAS is an attack knowledge base and the NIST AI RMF a risk framework; using one does not show compliance with the other.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a voluntary knowledge base as a certifiable standard, and D treats ATLAS coverage as compliance with a different framework.
Final two: A beats C because ATLAS records known attacks and grows as new ones appear; rating listed techniques better cannot cover attacks the catalog does not yet hold.
Exam cue: an attack catalog is a starting point for threat modeling, not a complete list; ask what covers attacks it does not yet hold.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. A pool-supplies assistant's design
questions.question: A Croatian pool-supplies retailer requires a chemist to approve every AI-drafted answer on mixing chemicals; for speed, its design streams each answer to customers as it is generated. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner hold each answer until a chemist clears it
options.B: Have a chemist watch answers stream and stop unsafe ones
options.C: Have the vendor confirm its model gives safe advice
options.D: Show customers a notice that each answer is AI-generated

questions.key_concept: Generative output streamed to users as it is produced cannot be reviewed first; where requirements demand prior human approval, the design must hold output.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against every fact in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Streaming shows customers each answer word by word as the model generates it, so no chemist can approve it first and the requirement fails by design. A wrong mixing instruction can release toxic gas. The owner should hold each answer until it is approved, even if replies slow down. Watching answers stream, option B, lets a chemist stop one, but customers have already read whatever streamed first.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a chemist can stop an unsafe answer mid-stream. But each word reaches the customer's screen as generated, so unsafe text is read before it is stopped.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But a vendor's assurance is a claim, not a control, and the requirement calls for a chemist's approval of each answer.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because telling customers about AI is good practice. But a notice stops no wrong instruction; customers still act on unapproved answers.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on the vendor's own claim about its model, and D adds a notice that stops no wrong answer reaching customers.
Final two: A beats B because streamed text is on the customer's screen as it is generated; a chemist who stops an answer mid-stream acts after part of it is read.
Exam cue: when a requirement puts a person between AI output and the people it affects, check the design gives that person the chance to act.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. An agent that merges records
questions.question: A Zambian health insurer plans an AI agent that merges 30,000 pairs of duplicate member records and permanently deletes the extras; it merged 99% of test pairs correctly. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent may invent members found in no source record
options.B: Some 300 wrong merges could mix two members' medical histories
options.C: The 99% may not hold on live records unlike the test pairs
options.D: The agent may retrain itself on each pair it merges

questions.key_concept: Even a highly accurate agent makes many errors at scale; when its actions delete data, the design must let each action be checked or undone.
questions.pre_read: Read each option against every fact in the stem before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: Even if the 99% holds, about 300 of 30,000 merges would be wrong, each joining two people's medical histories, and deleting the extras may leave no clean copy to separate them. The design needs a way to review or undo merges before anything is deleted. Whether 99% holds on live records, option C, is worth testing, but a perfect retest would still predict hundreds of hard-to-reverse errors.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generative AI can invent content. But this agent joins and deletes existing records; the stated risk is wrong joins, not new records.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because test results may not transfer. But even if 99% holds exactly, hundreds of wrong merges remain, and deletion makes them hard to reverse.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because agents seem to learn as they act. But merging records does not retrain the agent's model unless someone retrains it.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes acting retrains the agent, and A gives a record-merging agent a content-inventing failure.
Final two: B beats C because 1% of 30,000 is about 300 wrong merges even if the test rate holds, and deletion makes them hard to undo.
Exam cue: multiply an AI's error rate by its volume; when its actions delete or move data, ask how errors get reversed.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A vendor model answering guest reviews
questions.question: An Egyptian hotel group's review-reply model, from a vendor, learns weekly from all clients' ratings of its replies, guest names removed; the group validated it at purchase. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Each guest review may retrain the model as it is answered
options.B: The group's ratings may reveal guests' details to other clients
options.C: Guests may not be told that the replies are AI-written
options.D: Other clients' ratings can change its replies with no release

questions.key_concept: A vendor model that keeps learning from all clients' feedback changes without a release, so one buyer's validation at purchase soon describes a different model.
questions.pre_read: Rank the concerns by likelihood and impact before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that learns weekly from every client's ratings changes every week without any release or notice, steered by clients the group cannot see, including any that rate carelessly or maliciously. Replies to its guests can drift far from what it validated at purchase. Guests' details leaking through ratings, option B, is a fair question, but guest names are removed before learning, while weekly change is built into the design.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because AI is assumed to learn from everything it reads. But the stem says it learns weekly from ratings, not from each review it answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because shared learning can leak data between clients. But guest names are removed before learning, while unannounced weekly change is part of the design.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because telling guests about AI matters. But disclosure does not keep the replies within what the group validated.

tips: Eliminate: C is a disclosure point that leaves the replies as they are, and A misreads what the model learns from.
Final two: D beats B because the design changes the model weekly through clients the group cannot see; with names removed, the leak is the weaker concern.
Exam cue: a vendor model that keeps learning from shared feedback changes without releases; validation at purchase soon expires.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A chatbot that asks for personal details
questions.question: A Colombian aquarium's visitor chatbot, built on a general-purpose model, asks visitors for ID numbers and home addresses on its own, though no answer requires them. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt the chat logs that hold visitors' details
options.B: Have the owner add a privacy notice to the chat window
options.C: Have the owner confirm its prompt asks for none of these
options.D: Have the owner add checks that block such requests in replies

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design starts with collecting less; a generative chatbot can ask for personal data no task needs unless its design stops it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option against the facts the stem gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Nobody needs these details for visitor questions, yet the chatbot gathers them because a general-purpose model writes its own follow-up questions. Privacy by design stops the collection with tested checks outside the model that block such requests. Checking that its prompt never asks for these, option C, confirms intent, but the model writes its own questions, so only design limits and tests show it stops asking.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored data. But the chatbot would still collect details no task needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because notices make collection transparent. But telling visitors about needless collection does not make it necessary or stop it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a chatbot's prompt seems to set its behavior. But it asks on its own; a clean prompt cannot stop a general-purpose model writing its own questions.

tips: Eliminate: A secures data that should not be held, and B discloses collection instead of ending it.
Final two: D beats C because a general-purpose model writes its own follow-up questions; a clean prompt shows intent, while checks that block the requests stop the collection.
Exam cue: when an AI system gathers personal data its purpose never needs, fix the collection before storage, display or retention.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure requests at an electronics retailer
questions.question: A Tunisian electronics retailer retrained its reply model from scratch without chats customers asked to erase; a small model trained on the old version's replies serves its app. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The retrained model may still reproduce the erased chats
options.B: Erasure records may not show when each request was completed
options.C: The small model may still carry details from the erased chats
options.D: The small model may learn from chats on each customer's own phone

questions.key_concept: A model trained to imitate another can inherit what it memorized; erasure must reach every model derived from the old version.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each concern against what the stem says was done.
questions.correct_explanation: Training a small model to imitate another can pass on what the larger one learned, so details memorized from the erased chats may survive in the copy still running in the app. Retraining from scratch met the erasure duty for that model only. Gaps in erasure records, option B, weaken the evidence, but complete records would still miss data surviving in the small model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because models can memorize training text. But this model was retrained from scratch without the erased chats, so they are not in what it learned.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because erasure needs proof of completion. But complete records cannot show what the small model still holds; it learned from the old version's replies.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because on-phone models can adapt. But nothing in the stem says this one learns on phones; it learned from the old model's replies.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes on-phone learning the stem never mentions, and A is answered by the retraining, which left the erased chats out.
Final two: C beats B because a model copied from the old one can inherit what it learned; complete erasure records would still miss data surviving in the copy.
Exam cue: after an erasure, trace every model built from the affected version, including copies trained on its outputs.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Selling a model under the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: A Turkish software firm selling care homes a pressure-sore risk model applies the NIST AI RMF; senior management has accepted the residual risks in its register. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the firm document the residual risks for homes and staff
options.B: Have the firm drop accepted residual risks from the register
options.C: Have the firm add an owner and review date to each risk
options.D: Have the firm publish the model's overall accuracy for homes

questions.key_concept: Under the NIST AI RMF, residual risks to buyers and end users are documented to inform them, not kept in an internal register.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with what the framework expects.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance is not the end: MANAGE 1.4 asks for negative residual risks to downstream acquirers and end users to be documented, and the AI RMF says that documentation should inform end users of potential negative impacts. Care homes and their staff decide how far to rely on the model and cannot judge that from the firm's register. Adding owners and review dates, option C, strengthens that register but tells the homes and their staff nothing.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accepted risks seem settled. But accepted risks stay on the register to be monitored and reviewed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because accepted risks need owners and review dates. But a better register stays inside the firm; homes and staff still lack what they need to rely on the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because published performance helps buyers. But one accuracy figure hides the specific risks left over, such as residents the model misjudges.

tips: Eliminate: B drops risks that still need monitoring, and D shares a headline figure instead of the risks that remain.
Final two: A beats C because the framework expects residual risks shared with those who buy and use the model; a tidier internal register tells them nothing.
Exam cue: when an organization sells AI, the NIST AI RMF looks for residual risks documented for buyers and end users.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. An inventory at a software firm
questions.question: An Estonian school-software firm's AI inventory lists only the AI tools its staff use; its product's dropout-warning feature, sold to 300 schools, is not listed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the firm give buying schools a model card for the feature
options.B: Have the AI program owner list product AI in the inventory
options.C: Leave the feature to each buying school's own AI inventory
options.D: Have the IS auditor assign the feature's risk tier for now

questions.key_concept: The AI inventory covers AI the organization builds, buys or sells, not only the tools its staff use.
questions.pre_read: Ask who answers for each part of the system named in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: The inventory covers AI the organization builds, buys or sells. A dropout warning shapes how 300 schools treat students, and the firm answers for the model it ships: its data, validation, monitoring and updates. Without an entry it has no owner, tier or review. A model card for schools, option A, informs buyers, but it gives the feature no owner, tier or review inside the firm.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because buyers need documentation. But a model card informs schools; it gives the firm's own feature no owner, tier or review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because schools deploy the feature. But schools' entries cover their own use; the firm still answers for the model it builds and ships.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor understands the risk. But tiering is management's decision; the IS auditor assesses the inventory rather than filling it.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the firm's own product to its buyers' inventories, and D has the IS auditor make management's tiering decision.
Final two: B beats A because the firm must govern the AI in its products through its own inventory; a model card informs buyers but assigns no owner or review.
Exam cue: the AI inventory covers what the organization builds, buys and sells, not only the tools its staff use.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. A committee approval and a tolerance
questions.question: An Indian state's AI governance committee will approve a ration-card fraud model flagging 3% of honest households, over senior management's 1% tolerance, expecting a fix from retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the data team set a 3% tolerance for this model
options.B: Have the IS auditor accept the 3% rate on senior management's behalf
options.C: Have the committee refer the decision to senior management
options.D: Have the committee approve it, tracking the retrain monthly

questions.key_concept: A use that breaches senior management's tolerance needs senior management's decision; an AI governance committee cannot accept the breach itself.
questions.pre_read: Note who holds each role named in the stem.
questions.correct_explanation: Senior management set the 1% tolerance, so only it, or the board above it, can decide to run a model that breaches it. A retrain is a change whose results are unknown until tested, so an expected fix does not cure today's breach, and honest households would be flagged at three times the accepted rate. The committee should refer the decision. Approval with monthly tracking, option D, still accepts a breach the committee cannot accept.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because builders know what the model can achieve. But tolerances express how much harm is accepted, which senior management sets, not the data team.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IS auditor knows the test results. But accepting risk would make the IS auditor own a decision they must assess.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tracking keeps the fix on schedule. But a retrain's results are unknown until tested, and approval would still accept a breach the committee cannot accept.

tips: Eliminate: A lets builders set the limit their model must meet, and B has the IS auditor accept risk.
Final two: C beats D because a use that breaches senior management's tolerance needs senior management's decision; conditions on approval do not give the committee that authority.
Exam cue: when an AI use would run outside a tolerance, look for escalation to whoever set the tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A hosted chatbot's contract
questions.question: An Omani money-exchange firm's contract forbids probing its vendor-hosted customer chatbot, set up with its transfer guides, for harmful answers; the vendor shares a red-team summary. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the firm secure the right to run its own adversarial tests
options.B: Have the IS auditor probe the chatbot despite the contract
options.C: Have the firm obtain an independent red-team report on the vendor's model
options.D: Have the firm accept the summary, as vendors know their models

questions.key_concept: How a hosted chatbot fails depends on the buyer's own setup, so the buyer needs the right to test the system as deployed.
questions.pre_read: Compare what each option would let the firm know.
questions.correct_explanation: The firm answers for what its chatbot tells customers, and how a hosted chatbot fails depends on the firm's own setup: its transfer guides, customers and likely misuse, which the vendor's summary may not reflect. Only the firm's own adversarial testing, which the contract now forbids, shows how this deployment fails. An independent report on the vendor's model, option C, removes the vendor's bias but still tests the model, not the firm's deployment.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IS auditor gathers direct evidence. But testing in breach of the contract is not the IS auditor's call; the gap is the firm's missing testing right.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because independent testing beats the vendor's own. But a test of the vendor's model still misses the firm's own setup, transfer guides and customers' likely misuse.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors know their models best. But the vendor's tests reflect its own choices, not the misuse the firm's own customers might attempt.

tips: Eliminate: D takes the vendor's view as assurance, and B has the IS auditor test in breach of the contract.
Final two: A beats C because how a hosted chatbot fails depends on the firm's own setup; even independent tests of the vendor's model do not show that.
Exam cue: for hosted AI, look for the buyer's right to test the system as deployed, not just the vendor's reports.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. A call-recording notice and model training
questions.question: A Trinidadian gas utility plans to fine-tune a reply model on recorded customer calls; callers were told calls are recorded 'for quality and training purposes'. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt the call recordings before training begins
options.B: Have the privacy officer assess whether the notice covers AI training
options.C: Proceed, since callers agreed to model training by staying on
options.D: Have the owner test the tuned model for repeating callers' details

questions.key_concept: A call notice that mentions training usually means staff training, so whether calls may train a model is settled before tuning or testing.
questions.pre_read: Note the priority word before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Training in a call notice is usually read as training staff, not building an AI model, so callers may never have been told their words would train one. Whether the notice covers this new purpose, and on what lawful basis, is the first question, and the privacy officer should answer it. Testing the tuned model for memorized details, option D, is sound, but it does not decide whether the calls may be used at all.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because recordings need protection. But encryption does not decide whether the planned use is permitted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the notice mentions training. But it most likely meant staff training; callers did not knowingly agree to model training.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tuned models can memorize what callers said. But leak tests make safer a use that may not be allowed; whether the calls may train a model comes first.

tips: Eliminate: C reads a staff-training notice as consent to model training, and A answers a permission question with encryption.
Final two: B beats D because whether the calls may train a model comes first; memorization tests protect a use that may not be permitted.
Exam cue: check that the notice people saw covers AI training before weighing how the data or the model is protected.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A measurement plan under the AI RMF
questions.question: A Guatemalan cash-transfer program using the NIST AI RMF will measure its targeting model's overall error rate this year, and its errors for Indigenous households next year. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner measure errors for Indigenous households first
options.B: Have the owner wait for complaints from Indigenous households instead
options.C: Keep the plan, since the overall error rate covers every household
options.D: Have the owner give every risk equal effort in one cycle

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF selects measurement approaches starting with the most significant risks, not the easiest metrics.
questions.pre_read: Compare each option with what the framework expects.
questions.correct_explanation: The AI RMF expects measurement to start with the most significant risks. An overall error rate can look low while errors fall mostly on Indigenous households, and wrongly leaving them out of cash transfers is the harm that matters most; a year's wait leaves it unmeasured while decisions continue. Keeping the plan, option C, seems enough because every household is counted, but a pooled rate cannot show who bears the errors.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complaints show harm. But excluded households may never complain, and waiting leaves the main risk unmeasured.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the overall rate counts every household. But a pooled rate can look low while errors fall mostly on Indigenous households, the most significant risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because complete coverage sounds thorough. But the framework asks for priority by significance, not equal effort on every risk.

tips: Eliminate: D spreads effort evenly instead of by significance, and B waits for complaints from people who may never be heard.
Final two: A beats C because an overall error rate can hide errors that fall on one group; the framework starts with the most significant risk.
Exam cue: when a plan measures overall errors now and a group's errors later, look for the group most at risk of harm to be measured first.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Switching a chatbot off after hours
questions.question: Only its owner may switch off a Namibian city's drought-rules chatbot; one Saturday it told residents watering was allowed, and IT spent 14 hours reaching the owner. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner let on-call staff disable it on set criteria
options.B: Have internal audit approve any shutdown made after hours
options.C: Have the chatbot learn from residents' complaints about errors
options.D: Have the owner get the vendor to block advice on watering

questions.key_concept: AI harm continues while people wait to approve a shutdown, so owners pre-authorize who may disengage a system, and on what criteria.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option changes the next time something goes wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Because only the owner could switch the chatbot off, it stayed live for the 14 hours IT spent reaching them, while residents could act on the wrong advice. Pre-authorizing on-call staff to disable it when set criteria are met lets harm be stopped within minutes, while the owner stays accountable. Having the vendor block watering advice, option D, fixes this one error but leaves the next harmful answer live just as long.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit is independent. But internal audit assesses controls; it never approves operating decisions such as switching AI off.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complaints reveal errors. But a deployed chatbot does not learn from complaints, and the harm continues meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it removes the harmful answer. But it fixes one error; the next harmful answer would stay live just as long.

tips: Eliminate: B gives internal audit an operating decision, and C assumes the chatbot learns from complaints.
Final two: A beats D because the gap is who may stop the AI and when; a filter for one error leaves that gap open.
Exam cue: for live AI harm, look for pre-agreed authority to disengage quickly, with the owner still accountable.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A model that refers some cases
questions.question: A Samoan disaster-relief fund's model decides high-confidence claims within a day and refers others to staff, who take six weeks; its risk assessment counts only wrong decisions. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Wrong decisions on confident claims may go unappealed
options.B: Referred cases may teach the model to grow less confident
options.C: Claimants rare in its training data may face most of the delays
options.D: Referring cases to staff may itself count as automated decision-making

questions.key_concept: Which cases a model refers depends partly on what its training data covered, so referral delays can fall unevenly on groups it saw less of.
questions.pre_read: Consider which concern the facts in the stem support.
questions.correct_explanation: Which claims a model is unsure about is not random: it depends partly on what its training data covered, so referrals, and their six-week wait, can cluster among claimants the data held few of, such as those from outer islands. An assessment counting only wrong decisions misses that harm. Unappealed wrong decisions, option A, would matter, but wrong decisions are already counted and nothing suggests appeals are missing; the delays go uncounted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because automated decisions need an appeal route. But the assessment already counts wrong decisions, and nothing suggests appeals are missing; the uncounted harm is the six-week delay.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because models seem to learn from feedback. But the model does not retrain itself from referred cases.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because automated-decision rules worry organizations. But a case a person decides is not a solely automated decision.

tips: Eliminate: B assumes the model learns from referrals by itself, and D treats a staff decision as automated.
Final two: C beats A because referral itself causes harm, and which cases get referred depends partly on what the training data covered; the assessment counts only wrong decisions.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. An impact assessment a law requires
questions.question: An AI law requires public bodies using high-risk AI to assess fundamental-rights impacts; a Luxembourg housing agency cites its data protection impact assessment for its high-risk tenant-priority model. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The vendor may not have done its own rights impact assessments
options.B: Non-privacy rights, such as non-discrimination, may be missed
options.C: The duty may start once the model has caused harm
options.D: The data protection assessment may be out of date for the model

questions.key_concept: A data protection impact assessment covers personal data; a fundamental-rights assessment also covers harms such as discrimination and loss of access to services.
questions.pre_read: Read the duty's wording before the options.
questions.correct_explanation: The law asks for an assessment of impact on fundamental rights, which reach beyond data protection to non-discrimination, access to housing and effective remedy. A data protection impact assessment examines personal data handling, so it may support the duty but can leave unassessed whether the model disadvantages some tenants. An outdated data protection assessment, option D, is a weakness, but even a current one would cover only data protection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors document their models. But the duty falls on the body using the AI, for its own use, whatever the vendor did.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because some legal duties follow incidents. But an impact assessment is done before use, to find harms before they happen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because assessments must be current. But a fully current data protection assessment still covers only data protection, not the wider rights the law names.

tips: Eliminate: C treats an up-front assessment as triggered by harm, and A looks to the vendor for a duty that falls on the agency.
Final two: B beats D because a data protection assessment, however current, does not cover rights such as non-discrimination that the law names.
Exam cue: map each legal duty to evidence that covers its full scope; a related assessment is not automatically the required one.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. An AI aid in gymnastics judging
questions.question: A Fijian gymnastics federation's two judges score each routine independently; both now see the same AI tool's suggested deductions before scoring. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The second judge's score may now add little to the first
options.B: The judges' scores may now differ from each other more often
options.C: The tool may be untested on the federation's own athletes
options.D: The tool may learn from each judge's final score

questions.key_concept: Two independent human checks lose their value when both people first see the same AI output, since its misses and emphasis shape both.
questions.pre_read: Read what changed in the scoring process before weighing the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Two judges score independently so that one judge's misses are caught by the other. If both first see the same AI deductions, they tend to look where the tool looks, so a fault it misses can be missed twice and their agreement stops confirming anything. Testing the tool on the federation's athletes, option C, matters, but even a well-tested tool would leave both scores leaning on one view.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a new tool changes how judges work. But a shared suggestion pulls both judges toward it, so agreement rises, not falls.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a tool needs testing on its real use. But a well-tested tool still makes both judges look where it looks.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tools seem to learn from use. But it learns only if someone retrains it on the scores.

tips: Eliminate: D assumes the tool learns from each score, and B expects more disagreement when a shared suggestion pulls both judges together.
Final two: A beats C because one shared AI view removes the independence the second judge exists for; testing the tool does not restore it.
Exam cue: when every reviewer sees the same AI output first, ask whether the reviews are still independent.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A KRI for an ID-check model
questions.question: A Gabonese betting site's KRI for its ID-check model is the share of sampled rejections staff overturn on screens showing the model's reasons; it stays below tolerance. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner double the sample of rejections staff review
options.B: Have staff judge each case before seeing the model's output
options.C: Have the data team retrain the model on the overturned cases
options.D: Have the data team set the tolerance the KRI reports against

questions.key_concept: People who see a model's output before judging tend to agree with it, so a KRI built on their reviews understates the model's errors.
questions.pre_read: Consider what each option would let the KRI show.
questions.correct_explanation: Staff who see a model's reasons tend to agree with it, a pattern called automation bias, so wrongful rejections they should overturn can stand and the KRI reads low. Judging each sampled case before seeing the model's output gives an error count independent of the model. Doubling the sample, option A, adds cases but repeats the same lean in every one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a larger sample gives a more reliable rate. But every added case is judged with the model's reasons in view, so the rate stays biased low.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because overturned cases are useful training data. But a retrain changes the model, not how the KRI is measured.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because data teams know the model. But tolerances are set by senior management within appetite; the data team supports measurement.

tips: Eliminate: C treats a retrain as fixing how the KRI is measured, and D gives a tolerance decision to the data team.
Final two: B beats A because reviewers shown a model's reasons lean toward agreeing with it, so a bigger sample repeats the lean; only judging before seeing the output measures errors independently.
Exam cue: when people check an AI's decisions to measure its errors, ask whether they saw its answer first.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A model tuned through a provider's service
questions.question: In 2024 a Bermudian reinsurance broker fine-tuned a provider's model on its treaty files through the provider's service; corrected versions of that base model have since been released. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Corrected versions may retrain the copy without testing
options.B: The provider may change the base model without notice
options.C: The copy may keep weaknesses later versions corrected
options.D: The provider's controls report may omit its tuning service

questions.key_concept: A fine-tuned copy stays on the base model version it was tuned from, so fixes the provider releases later do not reach it.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each concern assumes about how the copy works.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning creates a separate copy built on the base model as it stood in 2024; the provider's later fixed versions do not flow into it, so weaknesses corrected since may remain in the copy the broker uses. Unannounced changes, option B, matter for live hosted models, but this copy stays on its 2024 base until the broker fine-tunes again on a newer one.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fixes seem to spread automatically. But a tuned copy is separate; base fixes need a new tuning run.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because providers do update hosted models silently. But a tuned copy stays on its original base, so the gap is fixes it never gets.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor evidence. But such reports cover the provider's environment, not which model version the copy is built on.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes base fixes flow into a tuned copy, and D looks to a controls report for model-version facts.
Final two: C beats B because a tuned copy stays on the base version it was built from; provider fixes reach it only through retuning.
Exam cue: for a fine-tuned model, ask which base version it sits on and how provider fixes will reach it.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Voice assistants beside hospital beds
questions.question: A Seychellois hospital puts voice assistants beside its ward beds; each answers patients' requests and remembers past requests to personalize later answers. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Patients' voice recordings may be sent to the vendor abroad
options.B: Next patients may hear what earlier patients asked or shared
options.C: The assistants may mishear patients' requests in some accents
options.D: Each patient's requests may retrain the vendor's base model

questions.key_concept: An assistant that remembers past requests carries one user's personal details to the next person who uses the same device.
questions.pre_read: Follow one request from the moment it is spoken.
questions.correct_explanation: A memory that personalizes answers carries one patient's requests into the next stay unless it is cleared, so a new patient asking for a reminder may hear an earlier patient's name, medicines or appointments. Clearing memory at discharge is a privacy-by-design default. Recordings sent abroad, option A, need a transfer and contract review, but the memory exposes each patient's details to whoever uses the bed next.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because cross-border transfers need review. But the memory reveals details to strangers at the bedside, a more direct exposure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because speech models err more on some accents. But a misheard request is usually noticed and repeated, while remembered details reach a stranger unseen.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because assistants seem to learn from use. But remembering requests stores them; it does not retrain the base model.

tips: Eliminate: D confuses a memory with retraining, and C raises a misheard request, which people notice, rather than a hidden exposure.
Final two: B beats A because memory on a shared device passes one person's details to the next user; a transfer abroad needs review but reaches no stranger.
Exam cue: when an AI remembers past requests, ask who else uses the same device or account.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Retuning a report-comment model
questions.question: A Guinean school group's report-comment model passed extraction tests after three training passes over teachers' comments on pupils; it will be retuned on them for twelve passes, untested. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The retune may go live without change approval
options.B: Parents may need to consent again to each retune
options.C: After the retune, it may repeat more comments verbatim
options.D: Teachers' comments on pupils may be kept after the retune ends

questions.key_concept: Each extra training pass repeats every example, raising memorization, so earlier extraction tests do not cover a model trained for more passes.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask who could be harmed and how.
questions.correct_explanation: Each training pass shows the model every comment again, and repetition raises memorization, so a model tuned for twelve passes can repeat more of what teachers wrote about pupils. Extraction tests describe the version tested, not the retune, so the new version needs its own. Change approval, option A, matters, but an approval resting on the earlier tests would miss the added leakage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a retune is a change needing approval. But an approval relying on the earlier extraction tests would miss what twelve passes add.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because consent feels tied to each training run. But the retune changes how long the model trains, not the purpose; the risk is what it can repeat.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training data needs a retention limit. But keeping it while the model is in use can be justified; the new risk is in what the model outputs.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a retune for the same purpose as needing new consent, and D questions keeping training data, which can be justified while the model is in use.
Final two: C beats A because more passes raise memorization, so the earlier extraction tests no longer describe the model; an approval relying on them would miss it.
Exam cue: when training runs longer or repeats data, treat earlier memorization tests as stale.
